title: How Neural Networks Learn: Backpropagation
hook: A neural net learns by asking, for every weight, 'how much did you contribute to my mistake?' Backprop answers all of them at once.
key_points: A network is layers of weighted sums passed through nonlinearities.
A loss function scores how far the network's output is from the right answer.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute each weight's effect on the loss.
Gradient descent then nudges every weight to shrink the loss, repeating until it learns.
content_html: Grant Sanderson's 3Blue1Brown series gives one of the clearest visual explanations of how neural networks learn. A network passes inputs through layers of weighted sums and nonlinear functions to produce an output; a loss measures how wrong that output is; and backpropagation figures out how to adjust every weight to make the loss smaller.
extra_html:
How it works

Each layer multiplies its inputs by weights, sums them, and applies a nonlinearity. To learn, you compute the loss, then run backpropagation: applying the chain rule from calculus, it propagates the error backward through the layers to find the gradient — how much each weight nudged the loss up or down. Gradient descent uses those gradients to tweak the weights, and many repetitions later, the network has learned.

Why it matters

Backpropagation is the engine behind essentially every modern neural network, from image classifiers to large language models. Grasping it demystifies training: it's not magic, just calculus telling each parameter which way to move. The 3Blue1Brown visuals make the chain-rule bookkeeping genuinely intuitive instead of intimidating.
